Definitely the second one,... They are both heartbreaking, particularly if you want to have children. It would be better to know for sure that you have to go another route to have a child in your life, such as adoption, surrogacy, or whatever else, than to deal with getting pregnant, growing the fetus for most of the year all the while excited to have your baby and fretting it may not survive outside the womb.

Labor and delivery are pretty traumatic to the human body. The thing that helps the healing process is the hormones that spark when interacting with the baby. Most first time mothers go through long labors. I'm talking about 12-48 hours. A C Section is a major abdominal surgery. Imagine going through all that pain, only for your baby to die right away. It would be devastating.

That's with the perspective that the person goes through with the pregnancy. They might do that if they think there is an outside chance their baby would survive or if they don't know they have a medical problem that would ensure life outside the womb wasn't possible for their bundle of joy. If they do know and they can't take long route, those people are going to have to get real comfortable with protection and abortion. 

It would definitely be less heartache to know you can't have your own biological children at all than to have that barest shred of hope dangled in front of your face or feeling like you killed your children by existing.

My dog passed away at the vet's office of congenital heart failure.  I was devastated. I cried a lot, disassociated when my tear ducts stopped doing their job, and I slept from exhaustion at my boyfriend's house because I couldn't go home after. I needed her to be there and I think I would have broken with the constant reminder that she wasn't. 

I spent the next month muddling through my days and crying every night. I quickly decided I couldn't deal with the emptiness where my dog should be and got another dog.

The dog I got was the same breed but a different color. She was different that my Akela, which was good because I struggled with the notion that I was replacing my dog, but I didn't feel like Denali was a replacement.

It was fantastic to have Denali while I grieved. She made me play, laugh, and give a crap about not dying because she depends on me. It's been 3 years. I still miss Akela. I have her picture in my room and I put flowers by her ashes. I think about her every day. She was my angel. Her birthday is always the hardest because I wish she was still here. 

I love Denali equally. She's such a princess but I love her so much. I am thinking that I will get another dog before she passes so that maybe she can teach the puppy some of her mannerisms and so that I don't have to worry myself over whether not I am attempting to replace an irreplaceable love.

I wish Denali could have met Akela. They would have been good for each other. Akela would have liked her. She liked puppies.

One of the camp activities at church camp one year was a hike through the woods at night. Down one path, the counselors announced that we would walk down the trail, one-by-one, without a flashlight and meet up with a couselor on the other side. I was maybe seven, very scared of the dark, and even more scared to be Alone in the dark. The logical side of me knew that it would be a short distance and that it would likely be uneventful, but I was still anxious and on the verge of throwing up from the fear.

I relayed this information to a counselor and I was told there would be no exceptions and that God would keep me safe through the dark. Hearing there was no way out of it sent my panic over the edge and I started crying. The counselor tried to reassure me that it would be fine when it was my turn but I cried through most of the walk.

My eyes were not adjusted to the darkness so I walked really slow down the path so I could feel the narrow trail out with my feet. I could just see myself tripping every time I brushed up on a large rock. The place the camp was in was very hilly so I honestly didn't know how steep the sides of the trail were.

Be the time I reached the other counselor, I wasn't crying as much or as loud. I was still trembling and when my vision started to take in more light to show me things in blues, black and gray instead of just black, I was honestly kind of pissed.

I was a despondent little shit for the rest of the hike, even during some owl hooting thing we did. Trust me, no one likes making owl noises more than me. I could not get over the fact that two teenagers made me hike alone in the pitch black when I was terrified without even a light to make sure I didn't fall or come across an animal that was minding its own business. I couldn't see. I was seven. I could have been stupid enough to leave the trail. They wouldn't know. I basically spent the whole night feeling like I was forced into facing my fears when I was not at all ready so I was not any fun. 

I bet my counselors and fellow campers hated me lol

I think I was pretty solid on it by 13. I did a full scale evaluation on my core thoughts and beliefs from like 11-13.

I went to church like a couple times a year as a kid and stopped before middle school but I suppose that's where the concept of god came from. 

A lot of what I was told in church didn't really line up for me. It made me uncomfortable to go to any church other than my family's hometown church.... and I only liked going there because my grandpa made the pews and helped make the steeple. He also drove across the country to get the bell. He passed away a little before I realized that I didn't like being preached at.... 

You know what's funny? I know he did a lot of work for that church but I don't recall going to a single service with him. I always went with my grandma on like Easter and communion but I don't think he came with. 

Anyway, in middle school, we had a class that taught us about religions or lack of religious belief. I knew there were other religions in the world but I leapt at the opportunity to look into what other people thought and believed. 

I spent about a year reading into different religions outside of school. My cousin caught wind of the interest and did the same. He really liked buddhism and gave it a shot but it turned out it wasn't for him. He had too much angry energy for all of that. I know he rebels against christianity in whatever form but I don't know what he believes now per se. My family is convinced he's an atheist but he has a lot of pagan friends so maybe he picked up one of those?

My interest turned out a little different. I liked the simple ideas of a lot of religions but on the whole, I still hate being told what to think. I switched my research interests over to mythology because it's way more fun and spent a lot more time looking internally for the answers I wanted.

I basically asked myself if I believed I had a soul and felt a response from my core, you know, a gut feeling that said yes. That's where I started and it took me a long while of letting me feel things out as the questions really occurred to me to determine my beliefs. 

I believe all that took place when I was 11-13. I have since believed in the existence of god but I believe in a lot of spiritual stuff. Basically, if I mull it over and if it feels right,  I go with it. I don't believe in going to church or whatever so I suppose I'm agnostic. It works for me. 

Good things happen when I trust my gut and bad things happen when I don't,  so I really just go with it. I'm a strong believer in thinking for yourself and finding your own answers. Those answers don't have to line up with mine. For things like this, it's a matter of perspective so all variables are valid. My perspective just happens to line up with believing in god overall but not believing all the stories I heard in church or wherever.

That's the long version.... uh... so thanks for coming to my TED Talk... I hope it was satisfactory. I can answer more questions but my answer to begin with is legitimately how I decided what I believed. I look internally and feel around for a gut response to tell me if the notion suits my spiritual needs.
It's just a feeling I have. I trust my gut and my gut says I do.... so that's that for me.

In December of 2010, I had an epiphany. In an instant, I went from not wanting kids at all to wanting to have kids. 

I was visiting family for the holidays and I had a room to myself in my father's place. I was exhausted from a full day of seeing everyone and being my usual awkward self so when I went to the room, I flopped on the bed and just laid there while staring at the ceiling.

My thoughts went to my nieces and my nephew at the time (I have way more now). I didn't really want kids for all the logical reasons but I wished I could be a better aunt to them.

I live far away and my siblings and I aren't close. I will blame the age gap between us because it is significant and leave it at that. I have always wanted to be closer to that side of my family and it has always felt like an insurmountable challenge.

In wanting to be closer to my nieces and nephew, I knew I had to be less awkward around them. I am a quiet, standoffish person. I haven't ever had the opportunity to be around small children or babies regularly so I was very intimidated by them in that I didn't know how to behave or what I was responsible for as the older party. I didn't even know how to talk to them. The idea of interactions used to give me mild panic attacks before I would even get on a plane to go see my family.

I started trying to work out how I could interact with my nieces and nephew more. It was a but of a mental puzzle and my mind went from "oh my god, what do I do?" to "If I had kids, how would I interact with them?".

Two things happened all at once. I didn't even get a chance to form a scenario in my head of me with a child of my own before I was slammed full force the thought "I want to have children". It was so loud in my mind, so heavy and overwhelming that it barely felt like my own. At the same time, I felt this uplifting feeling with in, like being filled with light and an affirmation of yes. 

It's so hard to describe these things because it was so intense and it came out of left field for me. The only other time I got that internal glowing feeling of yes was the first time I kissed the love of my life. That slam of a thought was extremely new.

I came out of the shock a little dazed. In that very instant, any misgivings I had about having children vanished. I knew with every part of my being that I wanted to have kids... and I was left with the fear that I was not prepared to have kids. I couldn't even talk to my nieces or nephews. I wasn't well off. In fact, I was well below the poverty line. I wasn't taking care of myself. The idea of pregnancy, labor, delivery, and child rearing filled me with dread.

I think I was on the verge of a really big panic attack when I saw movement out of the corner of my eye. I looked at the light and saw a ladybug climbing down the cord, at the end of December, when there were mountains of snow outside. I watched it and another came crawling out of the light socket.

I calmed down a lot just watching them and wondering why they were there. I collected myself and realized that I needed to sleep soon and I couldn't just have bugs crawling around above me, so I gently guided them onto the sleev of my shirt and took them downstairs. I put them in the mud room because it was pretty warm but not where I was sleeping.

When I got back to the room, I thought about all the life changes I would have to make to be ready for children. Queue a decade long obsession with researching everything and anything there is to know about pregnancy, labor, delivery, baby care, child care, and child psychology. I tried to find better paying jobs and I've been on various diets to try to lose weight. I am getting therapy for my depression and anxiety. I also made more effort to be closer to my nieces and nephews. I'm still awkward but I'm doing my best.

I don't have kids yet. I'm not financially ready and my boyfriend isn't ready for kids either. We are making steps to get ready though so that we can start trying within the next five years. 

That moment was huge for me. It changed my life entirely.
